---
title: "03 · Multiple regression"
subtitle: "Week 1"
---

::: {.guiding-q}
What if there are several predictors?
:::

## In this session

- Partial effects: the effect of one predictor *holding the others constant*
- Why simple and multiple regression can give different answers
- Standardising predictors (z-transformation) and comparing effects
- Collinearity and variance inflation
- Diagnostics in multiple regression

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [Collinearity](../../glossary.qmd#collinearity), [z-transformation (standardisation)](../../glossary.qmd#z-transformation), [Centring](../../glossary.qmd#centring)
:::

## Learning goals

After this session you can

- fit and interpret a model with several predictors,
- explain why an estimate changes when another predictor is added,
- diagnose collinearity.

## Simulate first

Age and body size are correlated, but only age affects the response. The simple regression on size finds an "effect" that disappears once age is in the model.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
n    <- 200
age  <- rnorm(n)
size <- 0.7 * age + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7)       # size depends on age
y    <- 1 + 0.5 * age + rnorm(n)           # y depends on age only

round(coef(lm(y ~ size)), 2)               # size seems to matter ...
round(coef(lm(y ~ size + age)), 2)         # ... until age is controlled for
```
